problems.problem: Let $ABC$ be a triangle and $Q$ a point on the internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$. The circle $\omega_1$ is circumscribed to the triangle $BAQ$ and intersects the segment $AC$ at a point $P\ne C$. The circle $\omega_2$ is circumscribed to the triangle $CQP$. The radius of the circle $\omega_1$ is larger than the radius of $\omega_2$. The circle centred at $Q$ with radius $QA$ intersects the circle $\omega_1$ at the points $A$ and $A_1$. The circle centred at $Q$ with radius $QC$ intersects $\omega_1$ at the points $C_1$ and $C_2$. Prove that $\angle A_1BC_1=\angle C_2PA$.

Let $S$ be a set of positive integers. For any $a$ and $b$ in the set we have $\gcd(a,b)>1$. For any $a$, $b$ and $c$ in the set we have $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$. Is it possible that $S$ has $2012$ elements?
($\gcd(x,y)$ and $\gcd(x,y,z)$ stand for the greatest common divisor of the numbers $x$ and $y$, and of the numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$, respectively.)

Do there exist positive real numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$ such that
$$\begin{aligned}x^4+y^4+z^4&=13,\\ x^3y^3z+y^3z^3x+z^3x^3y&=6\sqrt3,\\ x^3yz+y^3zx+z^3xy&=5\sqrt3\,?\end{aligned}$$

Let $k$ be a positive integer. At the European Chess Cup every pair of players played a game in which somebody won (there were no draws). For any $k$ players there was a player against whom they all lost, and the number of players was the least possible for such $k$. Is it possible that at the Closing Ceremony all the participants were seated at a round table in such a way that every participant was seated next to both a person he won against and a person he lost against?

For a positive integer $m$ let $m?$ be the product of the first $m$ prime numbers. Determine whether there exist positive integers $m$ and $n$ with the following property:
$$m?=n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3).$$

Let $P$ be a point inside a triangle $ABC$. A line through $P$ parallel to $AB$ meets $BC$ and $CA$ at points $L$ and $F$, respectively. A line through $P$ parallel to $BC$ meets $CA$ and $BA$ at points $M$ and $D$ respectively, and a line through $P$ parallel to $CA$ meets $AB$ and $BC$ at points $N$ and $E$ respectively. Prove that
$$(PDBL)\cdot(PECM)\cdot(PFAN)=8\cdot(PFM)\cdot(PEL)\cdot(PDN),$$
where $(XYZ)$ and $(XYZW)$ denote the area of the triangle $XYZ$ and the area of the quadrilateral $XYZW$.

We are given a combination lock consisting of $6$ rotating discs. Each disc consists of the digits $0, 1, 2, \ldots, 9$, in that order (after the digit $9$ comes $0$). The lock is opened by exactly one combination. A move consists of turning one of the discs one digit in either direction, and the lock opens instantly if the current combination is correct. The discs are initially put in the position $000000$, and we know that this combination is not correct.
a) What is the least number of moves necessary to ensure that we have found the correct combination?
b) What is the least number of moves necessary to ensure that we have found the correct combination, if we know that none of the combinations $000000, 111111, 222222, \ldots, 999999$ is correct?

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be positive real numbers satisfying
$$\frac{a}{1+b+c}+\frac{b}{1+c+a}+\frac{c}{1+a+b}\ge\frac{ab}{1+a+b}+\frac{bc}{1+b+c}+\frac{ca}{1+c+a}.$$
Prove that
$$\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}{ab+bc+ca}+a+b+c+2\ge 2\left(\sqrt{ab}+\sqrt{bc}+\sqrt{ca}\right).$$

Which of the following claims are true, and which of them are false? If a claim is true you should prove it; if it is not, find a counterexample.
a) Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be real numbers such that $a^{2013}+b^{2013}+c^{2013}=0$. Then $a^{2014}+b^{2014}+c^{2014}=0$.
b) Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be real numbers such that $a^{2014}+b^{2014}+c^{2014}=0$. Then $a^{2015}+b^{2015}+c^{2015}=0$.
c) Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be real numbers such that $a^{2013}+b^{2013}+c^{2013}=0$ and $a^{2015}+b^{2015}+c^{2015}=0$. Then $a^{2014}+b^{2014}+c^{2014}=0$.

At each vertex of a regular $n$-gon $A_1A_2\ldots A_n$ there is a unique pawn. In each step it is allowed:
1. to move all pawns one step in the clockwise direction, or
2. to swap the pawns at the vertices $A_1$ and $A_2$.
Prove that by a finite series of such steps it is possible to swap the pawns at the vertices
a) $A_i$ and $A_{i+1}$ for any $1\le i<n$, while leaving all other pawns in their initial places;
b) $A_i$ and $A_j$ for any $1\le i<j\le n$, leaving all other pawns in their initial places.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle. The external and internal angle bisectors of $\angle CAB$ intersect the side $BC$ at $D$ and $E$, respectively. Let $F$ be a point on the segment $BC$. The circumcircle of the triangle $ADF$ intersects $AB$ and $AC$ at $I$ and $J$, respectively. Let $N$ be the midpoint of $IJ$ and $H$ the foot of the perpendicular from $E$ to $DN$. Prove that $E$ is the incentre of the triangle $AHF$.

Find all infinite sequences $a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots$ of positive integers such that
a) $a_{nm}=a_na_m$ for all positive integers $n$, $m$, and
b) there are infinitely many positive integers $n$ such that $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}=\{a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n\}$.

Let $m$, $n$, $p$ be fixed positive real numbers which satisfy $mnp=8$. Depending on these constants, find the minimum of
$$x^2+y^2+z^2+mxy+nxz+pyz,$$
where $x$, $y$, $z$ are arbitrary positive real numbers satisfying $xyz=8$. When is equality attained? Solve the problem for
a) $m=n=p=2$;
b) arbitrary (but fixed) positive real numbers $m$, $n$, $p$.

Let $d(n)$ denote the number of positive divisors of $n$. For a positive integer $n$ we define $f(n)$ as
$$f(n)=d(k_1)+d(k_2)+\ldots+d(k_m),$$
where $1=k_1<k_2<\cdots<k_m=n$ are all the divisors of the number $n$. We call an integer $n>1$ almost perfect if $f(n)=n$. Find all almost perfect numbers.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle. Let $B'$, $A'$ be points on the perpendicular bisectors of $AC$, $BC$ respectively such that $B'A\perp AB$ and $A'B\perp AB$. Let $P$ be a point on the segment $AB$ and $O$ the circumcentre of the triangle $ABC$. Let $D$, $E$ be points on $BC$, $AC$ respectively such that $DP\perp BO$ and $EP\perp AO$. Let $O'$ be the circumcentre of the triangle $CDE$. Prove that $B'$, $A'$ and $O'$ are collinear.

A grasshopper is jumping along the number line. Initially it is situated at zero. In the $k$-th step, the length of its jump is $k$.
a) If the jump length is even, then it jumps to the left, otherwise it jumps to the right (for example, first it jumps one step to the right, then two steps to the left, then three steps to the right, then four steps to the left, ...). Will it visit every integer at least once?
b) If the jump length is divisible by three, then it jumps to the left, otherwise it jumps to the right (for example, first it jumps one step to the right, then two steps to the right, then three steps to the left, then four steps to the right, ...). Will it visit every integer at least once?

Two circles $C_1$ and $C_2$ intersect at points $A$ and $B$. Let $P$, $Q$ be points on the circles $C_1$, $C_2$ respectively such that $|AP|=|AQ|$. The segment $PQ$ intersects the circles $C_1$ and $C_2$ at the points $M$, $N$ respectively. Let $C$ be the midpoint of the arc $BP$ of $C_1$ which does not contain the point $A$, and let $D$ be the midpoint of the arc $BQ$ of $C_2$ which does not contain the point $A$. Let $E$ be the intersection of $CM$ and $DN$. Prove that $AE$ is perpendicular to $CD$.
Prove that for every positive integer $n$ there exist $n$ distinct positive rational numbers the sum of whose squares equals $n$.

We call a pair of positive integers $(n,k)$ with $k>1$ a lovely couple if there exists an $n\times n$ table consisting of ones and zeros with the following properties:
• in every row there are exactly $k$ ones;
• for every two rows there is exactly one column such that at both intersections of that column with the mentioned rows the number one is written.
Solve the following subproblems:
a) Let $d\ne 1$ be a divisor of $n$. Determine all remainders that $d$ can give when divided by $6$.
b) Prove that there exist infinitely many lovely couples.

Find all pairs $(x,y)$ of integers that satisfy the equation
$$x^2y+y^2=x^3.$$

A regular hexagon in the plane is called sweet if its area is equal to $1$. Is it possible to place $2000000$ sweet hexagons in the plane such that the union of their interiors is a convex polygon of area at least $1900000$?
Remark: a subset $S$ of the plane is called convex if for every pair of points in $S$, every point of the straight line segment that joins the pair of points also belongs to $S$. The hexagons may overlap.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle. Denote by $H$ and $M$ the orthocentre of $ABC$ and the midpoint of the side $BC$, respectively. Let $Y$ be a point on $AC$ such that $YH$ is perpendicular to $MH$, and let $Q$ be a point on $BH$ such that $QA$ is perpendicular to $AM$. Let $J$ be the second point of intersection of $MQ$ and the circle with diameter $MY$. Prove that $HJ$ is perpendicular to $AM$.

The real numbers $x$, $y$, $z$ satisfy $x^2+y^2+z^2=3$. Prove the inequality
$$x^3-(y^2+yz+z^2)x+y^2z+yz^2\le 3\sqrt3$$
and find all triples $(x,y,z)$ for which equality holds.

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be non-zero real numbers such that
$$a^2+b+c=\frac1a,\qquad b^2+c+a=\frac1b,\qquad c^2+a+b=\frac1c.$$
Prove that at least two of $a$, $b$, $c$ are equal.

Find all pairs $(x,y)$ of positive integers such that
$$xy\mid x^2+2y-1.$$

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $|AB|<|AC|$ and orthocentre $H$. The circle with centre $A$ and radius $|AC|$ intersects the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ at the point $D$, and the circle with centre $A$ and radius $|AB|$ intersects the segment $AD$ at the point $K$. The line through $K$ parallel to $CD$ intersects $BC$ at the point $L$. If $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$ and $N$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $H$ to $AL$, prove that the line $MN$ bisects the segment $AH$.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Ana and Banana are playing the following game. First, Ana arranges $2n$ cups in a row on a table, each facing upside-down. She then places a ball under a cup and makes a hole in the table under some other cup. Banana then gives a finite sequence of commands to Ana, where each command consists of swapping two adjacent cups in the row. Her goal is to achieve that the ball has fallen into the hole during the game. Assuming Banana has no information about the position of the hole and the position of the ball at any point, what is the smallest number of commands she has to give in order to achieve her goal?

Every positive integer is marked with a number from the set $\{0,1,2\}$, according to the following rule: if a positive integer $k$ is marked with $j$, then the integer $k+j$ is marked with $0$. Let $S$ denote the sum of the marks of the first $2019$ positive integers. Determine the maximum possible value of $S$.

Define a sequence $x_1, x_2, x_3, \ldots$ such that $x_1=\sqrt2$ and
$$x_{n+1}=x_n+\frac{1}{x_n}\quad\text{for } n\in\mathbb{N}.$$
Prove that the following inequality holds:
$$\frac{x_1^2}{2x_1x_2-1}+\frac{x_2^2}{2x_2x_3-1}+\ldots+\frac{x_{2018}^2}{2x_{2018}x_{2019}-1}+\frac{x_{2019}^2}{2x_{2019}x_{2020}-1}>\frac{2019^2}{x_{2019}^2+\frac{1}{x_{2019}^2}}.$$

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with circumcircle $\omega$. Let $l_B$ and $l_C$ be two lines through the points $B$ and $C$, respectively, such that $l_B\parallel l_C$. The second intersections of $l_B$ and $l_C$ with $\omega$ are $D$ and $E$, respectively. Assume that $D$ and $E$ are on the same side of $BC$ as $A$. Let $DA$ intersect $l_C$ at $F$ and let $EA$ intersect $l_B$ at $G$. If $O$, $O_1$ and $O_2$ are the circumcentres of the triangles $ABC$, $ADG$ and $AEF$, respectively, and $P$ is the circumcentre of the triangle $OO_1O_2$, prove that $l_B\parallel OP\parallel l_C$.

Let $u$ be a positive rational number and $m$ a positive integer. Define a sequence $q_1, q_2, q_3, \ldots$ such that $q_1=u$ and for $n\ge 2$:
if $q_{n-1}=\frac ab$ for some relatively prime positive integers $a$ and $b$, then $q_n=\frac{a+mb}{b+1}$.
Determine all positive integers $m$ such that the sequence $q_1, q_2, q_3, \ldots$ is eventually periodic for every positive rational number $u$.
Remark: a sequence $x_1, x_2, x_3, \ldots$ is eventually periodic if there are positive integers $c$ and $t$ such that $x_n=x_{n+t}$ for all $n\ge c$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle. Let $D$ and $E$ be the midpoints of the sides $AB$ and $AC$ respectively. Let $F$ be the point such that $D$ is the midpoint of $EF$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of the triangle $FDB$. Let $G$ be a point on the segment $CD$ such that the midpoint of $BG$ lies on $\Gamma$. Let $H$ be the second intersection of $\Gamma$ and $FC$. Show that the quadrilateral $BHGC$ is cyclic.

Two types of tiles, depicted in the figure, are given. Find all positive integers $n$ such that an $n\times n$ board consisting of $n^2$ unit squares can be covered without gaps with these two types of tiles (rotations and reflections are allowed) so that no two tiles overlap and no part of any tile covers an area outside the $n\times n$ board.

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be positive real numbers such that $ab+bc+ac=a+b+c$. Prove the following inequality:
$$\sqrt{a+\frac bc}+\sqrt{b+\frac ca}+\sqrt{c+\frac ab}\le\sqrt2\cdot\min\left\{\frac ab+\frac bc+\frac ca,\ \frac ba+\frac cb+\frac ac\right\}.$$

We say that a quadruple of non-negative real numbers $(a,b,c,d)$ is balanced if
$$a+b+c+d=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2.$$
Find all positive real numbers $x$ such that
$$(x-a)(x-b)(x-c)(x-d)\ge 0$$
for every balanced quadruple $(a,b,c,d)$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle such that $|AB|<|AC|$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be points on the minor arc $BC$ of the circumcircle of $ABC$ such that $|BX|=|XY|=|YC|$. Suppose that there exists a point $N$ on the segment $AY$ such that $|AB|=|AN|=|NC|$. Prove that the line $NC$ passes through the midpoint of the segment $AX$.

Let $\ell$ be a positive integer. We say that a positive integer $k$ is nice if $k!+\ell$ is the square of an integer. Prove that for every positive integer $n\ge\ell$, the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, n^2\}$ contains at most $n^2-n+\ell$ nice integers.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Morgane has coloured the integers $1, 2, \ldots, n$. Each of them is coloured in exactly one colour. It turned out that for all positive integers $a$ and $b$ such that $a<b$ and $a+b\le n$, at least two of the integers among $a$, $b$ and $a+b$ are of the same colour. Prove that there exists a colour that has been used for at least $2n/5$ integers.

Find all positive integers $n$ for which there exist three positive divisors $a$, $b$, $c$ of $n$ such that $a>b>c$ and
$$a^2-b^2,\quad b^2-c^2,\quad a^2-c^2$$
are also divisors of $n$.

Find all pairs of positive real numbers $(x,y)$ such that $xy$ is an integer and
$$x+y=\lfloor x^2-y^2\rfloor.$$
Remark: for a real number $z$, we denote by $\lfloor z\rfloor$ the greatest integer not greater than $z$. Some examples are $\lfloor 17\rfloor=17$, $\lfloor 8.2\rfloor=8$ and $\lfloor -5.4\rfloor=-6$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $|BC|<|AC|$. Let $I$ be the incentre and $\tau$ the incircle of $ABC$, which touches $BC$ and $AC$ at the points $D$ and $E$, respectively. The point $M$ is on $\tau$ such that $BM$ is parallel to $DE$, and $M$ and $B$ are on the same side of the angle bisector of $\angle BCA$. Let $F$ and $H$ be the intersections of $\tau$ with $BM$ and $CM$ different from $M$, respectively. Let $J$ be a point on the line $AC$ such that $JM$ is parallel to $EH$. Let $K$ be the intersection of $JF$ and $\tau$ different from $F$. Prove that the lines $ME$ and $KH$ are parallel.

Let $X=\{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 300\}$. A collection $F$ of distinct (not necessarily non-empty) subsets of $X$ is lovely if for any three (not necessarily distinct) sets $A$, $B$, $C$ in $F$, at most three of the following eight sets are non-empty:
$$\begin{array}{cccc} A\cap B\cap C, & \overline{A}\cap B\cap C, & A\cap\overline{B}\cap C, & A\cap B\cap\overline{C},\\ \overline{A}\cap\overline{B}\cap C, & \overline{A}\cap B\cap\overline{C}, & A\cap\overline{B}\cap\overline{C}, & \overline{A}\cap\overline{B}\cap\overline{C},\end{array}$$
where $\overline{S}$ denotes the set of all elements of $X$ that are not in $S$. What is the greatest possible number of sets in a lovely collection?

Suppose $a$, $b$, $c$ are positive integers such that
$$\gcd(a,b)+\gcd(a,c)+\gcd(b,c)=b+c+2023.$$
Prove that $\gcd(b,c)=2023$.
Remark: for positive integers $x$ and $y$, $\gcd(x,y)$ denotes their greatest common divisor.

Let $n\ge 5$ be an integer. There are $n$ points in the plane, no three of them collinear. Each day, Tom erases one of the points, until there are three points left. On the $i$-th day, for $1\le i\le n-3$, before erasing that day's point, Tom writes down the positive integer $v(i)$ such that the convex hull of the points at that moment has $v(i)$ vertices. Finally, he writes down $v(n-2)=3$. Find the greatest possible value that the expression
$$|v(1)-v(2)|+|v(2)-v(3)|+\ldots+|v(n-3)-v(n-2)|$$
can attain over all possible initial configurations of $n$ points and all possible moves of Tom.
Remark: the convex hull of a finite set of points in the plane is the smallest convex polygon containing all the points of the set (inside it or on the boundary).

Consider an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ with $|AB|<|AC|$. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of the segments $BC$ and $AB$, respectively. The circle with diameter $AB$ intersects the lines $BC$, $AM$ and $AC$ at $D$, $E$ and $F$, respectively. Let $G$ be the midpoint of $FC$. Prove that the lines $NF$, $DE$ and $GM$ are concurrent.

We say that a $2023$-tuple of non-negative integers $(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{2023})$ is sweet if the following conditions hold:
• $a_1+a_2+\ldots+a_{2023}=2023$;
• $\frac{a_1}{2^1}+\frac{a_2}{2^2}+\ldots+\frac{a_{2023}}{2^{2023}}\le 1$.
Determine the greatest positive integer $L$ such that
$$a_1+2a_2+\ldots+2023a_{2023}\ge L$$
holds for every sweet $2023$-tuple $(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{2023})$.

Wiske wrote a $2024$-digit positive integer on the blackboard. In each round of the game she erases the last digit of the integer, say $d$, and writes down the sum of the remaining number and $2d$ in place of the old number. She repeats the same steps with the newly obtained number. After a certain number of rounds, Wiske found that the new number obtained was the same as the number in the previous round, and she stopped the game. What is the smallest possible $2024$-digit integer that Wiske could have started with in this game?

Let $X$ be the largest possible value of the expression
$$\min\{bc, 2-a^2\}+\min\{ac, 2-b^2\}+\min\{ab, 2-c^2\},$$
where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are positive real numbers. Similarly, let $Y$ be the smallest possible value of the expression
$$\max\{a^2, 2-bc\}+\max\{b^2, 2-ac\}+\max\{c^2, 2-ab\},$$
where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are positive real numbers. Prove that $X=Y$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with incentre $I$ and incircle $\omega$. Let $\ell$ be the tangent to $\omega$ parallel to $BC$ and distinct from $BC$. Let $D$ be the intersection of $\ell$ and $AC$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $ID$. Prove that $\angle AMD=\angle DBC$.

Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of (distinct) subsets of the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ such that for all $A, B\in\mathcal{F}$ we have $A^c\cup B\in\mathcal{F}$, where $A^c$ is the set of all members of $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ that are not in $A$. Prove that every $k\in\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ appears in at least half of the sets in $\mathcal{F}$.

problems.problem: Let $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ be two circles intersecting at $A$ and $B$. The common tangent of $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ closer to $A$ touches $\omega_1$ at $P$ and $\omega_2$ at $Q$. The tangent to $\omega_1$ at $A$ meets $\omega_2$ at $C$, different from $A$, and the extension of $AP$ meets $QC$ at $D$. Let $E$ be the circumcentre of the triangle $ABD$. The lines $AD$ and $QE$ intersect at $F$. Prove that $F$ lies on the circle with diameter $PQ$.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Divide an equilateral triangle of side length $n$ into equilateral triangles of side length one (the upper part of the figure shows the case $n=4$). Label the small equilateral triangles through which one of the altitudes of the large equilateral triangle passes as $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ (see the upper part of the figure for how to do this in the case $n=4$). Let $f(i)$ denote the number of ways to tile the large equilateral triangle, with the triangle $a_i$ removed, using exactly one of each of the pieces shown in the lower part of the figure (the trapezoids formed by a row of $3, 5, \ldots, 2n-1$ unit triangles, whose parallel sides have lengths $1$ and $2$, $2$ and $3$, $\ldots$, $n-1$ and $n$).
• If $n$ is even, determine $f(2)+f(4)+\cdots+f(2k)+\cdots+f(n)$.
• Prove that $f(1)+f(2)+\cdots+f(n)\ge 2^{n-2}$ for all positive integers $n$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/emcj_2025_p2_fig.png

Determine the largest positive integer $n$ for which there exist positive integers $a$ and $q$ such that
$$q^6\le n\quad\text{and}\quad\left|\sqrt2-\frac aq\right|\le\frac{1}{\sqrt n}.$$

Find all positive integers $n$ with the following property: for every positive integer $d$ which divides $n$, there exists a positive integer $k$ which divides $n$ such that
$$d+n\mid dn+k.$$
